newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma general blames communists, NLD for unrest.
newsitem.headline: Burma general blames communists, NLD for unrest.

text.p: A top Burmese general on Tuesday said the government had arrested 47 political activists in connection with recent unrest and blamed Communists and opposition politicians for trying to destabilise the country.

Lieutenant-General Khin Nyunt, Secretary One of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), told a rare news conference the government had arrested 34 members of the outlawed Burma Communist Party (BCP) and 13 National League for Democracy (NLD) members in the wake of student unrest this month.

"We have uncovered who was behind the student unrest and other recent destructive activities in the country," he told the news briefing in which the government presented a 60-page report on the findings of an investigation into the unrest.

"So far we have arrested 34 BCP underground agents and 13 NLD members for their involvement in creating the unrest," he said, adding that three wanted BCP agents were still at large, two of whom were university students.
The BCP, formerly a key political force led by Thakin Than Tun -- an uncle of NLD leader Aung San Suu Kyi -- was outlawed after Burma became independent in 1948.

The opposition NLD, co-founded in 1988 by Nobel Peace laureate Suu Kyi, won a landslide election victory in 1990 but was not allowed to take power after SLORC refused to recognise the results of the poll.
Nearly 2,000 university students took to the streets in early December for a series of anti-government demonstrations that were the biggest in Rangoon since 1988.
The government briefly detained more than 860 students who were protesting against police brutality and demanding political freedom and rights.
Khin Nyunt said nine civilians who were arrested following the recent demonstrations had been released.
SLORC officials have accused exiled students, outlawed Burmese Communists and the NLD of instigating the protests. The NLD and the Thailand-based exiles have denied involvement.
Khin Nyunt said universities in Rangoon, closed in the wake of the protests, would be reopened but did not say when.

He also blamed the Karen National Union (KNU) -- an ethnic guerrilla group based in jungles near the Thai-Burma border -- and exiled dissidents for two time-bomb blasts last week at a Buddhist site in a Rangoon suburb that killed five people and injured 17.

"We have information that a group of destructive elements were sent through jungle roads to conspire with above-ground elements," he said. "But we never thought they would do such a dirty, wicked, inhumane act at such a sacred and holy place."
"Ignoring the fact that their acts would injure and kill innocent...people, they carried it out with the main purpose of ruining SLORC's dignity," he said.
The predominantly Christian KNU said in a statement obtained in Bangkok tjat it had no connection to the bombings.
Khin Nyunt urged all Burmese people, and students in particular, to cooperate with the government to prevent further unrest and "destructive elements" in Burma.
Top government officials routinely refer to Suu Kyi and the NLD as "destructive elements" and have repeatedly called for them to be annihilated.
